items.definition: To remove a need or difficulty in advance, so that it never has to be dealt with.
items.etymology: From Late Latin obviare 'to meet in the way, to prevent', built from ob 'against' and via 'way'.
items.example_sentence: Automated backups obviate the need to remember a weekly export.

items.definition: Lasting only a very short time; quickly fading or passing away.
items.etymology: From Greek ephemeros 'lasting only a day', from epi 'on' and hemera 'day'.
items.example_sentence: Most social-media trends are ephemeral, gone within a week.

items.definition: Cheerfully optimistic, especially about an outcome that others may doubt.
items.etymology: From Latin sanguineus 'of blood'; in medieval humoral theory a blood-dominant temperament was thought to make a person confident and hopeful.
items.example_sentence: The team stayed sanguine about the launch despite two failed tests.

items.definition: Using very few words; brief to the point of seeming terse.
items.etymology: From Greek Lakonikos 'of Laconia', the region around Sparta, whose people were known for blunt brevity of speech.
items.example_sentence: Her laconic reply, 'Fine,' ended the discussion.

items.definition: Present, appearing or found everywhere at the same time.
items.etymology: From Latin ubique 'everywhere', via the theological term ubiquity.
items.example_sentence: Smartphones became ubiquitous within a decade of their introduction.

items.definition: Causing serious harm in a gradual or hidden way.
items.etymology: From Latin perniciosus 'destructive', from pernicies 'ruin', from per 'completely' and nex 'death'.
items.example_sentence: Small daily distractions can have a pernicious effect on deep work.

items.definition: Excessively talkative, especially about unimportant matters.
items.etymology: From Latin garrulus 'chattering', from garrire 'to chatter'.
items.example_sentence: A garrulous seatmate turned the short flight into a long one.

items.definition: Calmness and evenness of temper, especially under stress.
items.etymology: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus 'even, level' and animus 'mind'.
items.example_sentence: She received the unexpected results with equanimity and simply reran the analysis.

items.definition: To make something less severe, serious or painful without removing it entirely.
items.etymology: From Latin mitigare 'to soften', from mitis 'mild' and agere 'to make, to drive'.
items.example_sentence: Daily backups mitigate the risk of losing journal entries.

items.definition: Clear, logical and convincing.
items.etymology: From Latin cogent-, the present participle stem of cogere 'to compel', from co- 'together' and agere 'to drive'.
items.example_sentence: The reviewer found the second argument far more cogent than the first.

items.definition: Brisk and cheerful readiness to do something.
items.etymology: From Latin alacritas, from alacer 'brisk, lively'.
items.example_sentence: He accepted the invitation with an alacrity that surprised everyone.

items.definition: Done routinely and with minimal effort, only to get it over with.
items.etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius 'careless', from perfungi 'to get through, to discharge', from per 'through' and fungi 'to perform'.
items.example_sentence: A perfunctory code review missed the obvious bug.

items.definition: A person who flatters someone powerful in order to gain advantage.
items.etymology: Via Latin from Greek sykophantes 'informer', literally 'fig-shower' (sykon 'fig' + phainein 'to show'); why figs were involved is uncertain.
items.example_sentence: The director surrounded herself with sycophants and stopped hearing bad news.

items.definition: Excessively eager to please or obey.
items.etymology: From Latin obsequiosus, from obsequium 'compliance', from ob 'toward' and sequi 'to follow'.
items.example_sentence: The waiter's obsequious attention made the dinner uncomfortable.

items.definition: Stubbornly resistant to authority, control or treatment.
items.etymology: From Latin recalcitrare 'to kick back', from re- 'back' and calx 'heel'.
items.example_sentence: A recalcitrant dependency kept breaking the build after every update.

items.definition: Just begun and not yet fully formed or developed.
items.etymology: From Latin inchoatus, past participle of inchoare 'to begin'.
items.example_sentence: The plan was still inchoate, little more than a list of ideas.

items.definition: Idealistic to an impractical degree; pursuing noble but unrealistic goals.
items.etymology: From Don Quixote, the idealistic hero of Miguel de Cervantes's novel (1605-1615) who attacks windmills he believes are giants.
items.example_sentence: His quixotic plan to read every book in the library lasted a month.

items.definition: Eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.
items.etymology: From Latin truculentus 'fierce, savage', from trux 'fierce'.
items.example_sentence: The truculent caller refused every solution the agent offered.

items.definition: Experienced through imagining another person's actions or feelings rather than directly.
items.etymology: From Latin vicarius 'substitute', from vicis 'change, turn, place'.
items.example_sentence: Travel videos give a vicarious thrill to people who cannot leave home.

items.definition: Having or showing keen judgment and practical wisdom.
items.etymology: From Latin sagax 'of keen perception', related to sagire 'to perceive keenly'.
items.example_sentence: A sagacious mentor knows when to stay silent and let you find the error.

items.definition: To make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better.
items.etymology: From French ameliorer, from Latin melior 'better'.
items.example_sentence: Better lighting ameliorated the eye strain from long study sessions.

items.definition: Lacking imagination or excitement; ordinary and matter-of-fact.
items.etymology: From Late Latin prosaicus 'in prose', from prosa 'prose', contrasted with the heightened language of poetry.
items.example_sentence: The breakthrough had a prosaic cause: someone finally read the manual.

items.definition: Holding firmly to a goal, position or grip; persistent.
items.etymology: From Latin tenax 'holding fast', from tenere 'to hold'.
items.example_sentence: Only a tenacious learner keeps a streak alive for a full year.

items.definition: To calm someone's anger or reduce their hostility, often by concessions.
items.etymology: From Latin placare 'to calm, to appease'.
items.example_sentence: A refund was enough to placate the frustrated customer.

items.definition: To drain someone of energy or vitality. Often misused to mean the opposite, 'to energize'.
items.etymology: From Latin enervare 'to weaken', from e- 'out of' and nervus 'sinew'.
items.example_sentence: The humid afternoon enervated the whole hiking group.

items.definition: Understood by or intended for only a small group with specialized knowledge.
items.etymology: From Greek esoterikos 'belonging to an inner circle', from esotero 'further inward'.
items.example_sentence: The talk drifted into esoteric details of compiler design.

items.definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; hard to please.
items.etymology: From Latin fastidiosus 'disdainful', from fastidium 'loathing, squeamishness'.
items.example_sentence: A fastidious editor caught every inconsistent date in the manuscript.

items.definition: Proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects.
items.etymology: From Latin insidiosus 'cunning', from insidiae 'ambush', from insidere 'to sit in or on'.
items.example_sentence: Scope creep is insidious because each small addition seems harmless.

items.definition: Most noticeable or important; standing out from the rest.
items.etymology: From Latin salient-, present participle stem of salire 'to leap'; the sense moved from 'leaping' to 'jutting out' to 'prominent'.
items.example_sentence: The summary lists only the salient findings of the study.

items.definition: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and without apparent reason.
items.etymology: From French capricieux, from Italian capriccio; probably capo 'head' + riccio 'hedgehog', hair standing on end in fright, though the origin is disputed.
items.example_sentence: Capricious spring weather made the outdoor event hard to plan.

items.definition: Stated or appearing to be true, though possibly not the real reason or situation.
items.etymology: Via French from Medieval Latin ostensibilis, from Latin ostendere 'to show', from ob 'before' and tendere 'to stretch'.
items.example_sentence: The ostensible purpose of the meeting was budgeting, but everyone expected layoffs.

items.definition: To regard with deep respect, often bordering on reverence.
items.etymology: From Latin venerari 'to worship, to revere'.
items.example_sentence: Many physicists venerate Feynman's lectures as a model of clear teaching.

items.definition: Angry and bitter in tone, especially in a dispute.
items.etymology: From Latin acrimonia 'sharpness', from acer 'sharp, keen'.
items.example_sentence: The partnership ended in an acrimonious dispute over credit.

items.definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something at the same time.
items.etymology: From German Ambivalenz, coined by the psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler around 1910 from Latin ambi- 'both' and valentia 'strength'.
items.example_sentence: She felt ambivalent about the promotion: more pay, but far less research time.

items.definition: To persuade someone through flattery, gentle pressure or repeated coaxing.
items.etymology: From French cajoler 'to coax'; the earlier history of the French word is uncertain.
items.example_sentence: He cajoled his roommate into joining the morning runs.

items.definition: The quality of being open, honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
items.etymology: From Latin candor 'whiteness, brightness', from candere 'to shine'; the sense moved from purity to frankness.
items.example_sentence: The reviewer's candor about the flawed method improved the final paper.

items.definition: Careful to consider all circumstances and risks before acting or speaking.
items.etymology: From Latin circumspectus, past participle of circumspicere 'to look around', from circum 'around' and specere 'to look'.
items.example_sentence: Be circumspect about sharing preliminary results before peer review.

items.definition: A confusing and difficult problem or question with no obvious answer.
items.etymology: Recorded from the 1590s; origin unknown, possibly a mock-Latin coinage from university slang.
items.example_sentence: Balancing privacy with useful data collection is a real conundrum.

items.definition: Causing harm or damage, often in a way that is not immediately obvious.
items.etymology: From Greek deleterios 'noxious', from deleisthai 'to hurt, to injure'.
items.example_sentence: Chronic sleep loss has deleterious effects on memory consolidation.

items.definition: Intended to teach or instruct, sometimes in a way that feels preachy.
items.etymology: From Greek didaktikos 'apt at teaching', from didaskein 'to teach'.
items.example_sentence: The documentary was informative but too didactic to be enjoyable.

items.definition: Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence.
items.etymology: From Latin diffidere 'to mistrust', from dis- 'not' and fidere 'to trust'.
items.example_sentence: The diffident student had the best answer but almost didn't share it.

items.definition: Essentially different in kind; not easily compared or combined.
items.etymology: From Latin disparatus 'separated', past participle of disparare, from dis- 'apart' and parare 'to prepare, arrange'.
items.example_sentence: The report merges data from disparate sources into one table.

items.definition: Cheerful and full of energy; bubbling over with enthusiasm.
items.etymology: From Latin ebullire 'to boil over', from e- 'out' and bullire 'to boil'.
items.example_sentence: An ebullient host kept the conversation moving all evening.

items.definition: Drawing ideas, styles or tastes from a broad and diverse range of sources.
items.etymology: From Greek eklektikos 'selective', from eklegein 'to pick out'.
items.example_sentence: Her reading list is eclectic, mixing physics, poetry and economics.

items.definition: Outstandingly bad; shocking in how obvious the error or offense is.
items.etymology: From Latin egregius 'standing out from the flock', from e- 'out of' and grex 'flock'; the sense shifted from 'remarkably good' to 'remarkably bad'.
items.example_sentence: Plotting only the favorable months was an egregious misuse of the data.

items.definition: To make something clear by explaining it in detail.
items.etymology: From Late Latin elucidare 'to make light', from e- 'out' and lucidus 'bright'.
items.example_sentence: A single diagram elucidated what three pages of text had obscured.

items.definition: Having or showing great knowledge gained from extensive study.
items.etymology: From Latin eruditus 'instructed', past participle of erudire, from e- 'out of' and rudis 'untrained, rough'.
items.example_sentence: His erudite footnotes were longer than the chapters themselves.

items.definition: To make an existing problem, situation or feeling worse.
items.etymology: From Latin exacerbare 'to irritate, provoke', from ex- 'thoroughly' and acerbus 'harsh, bitter'.
items.example_sentence: Skipping the warm-up exacerbated the old knee injury.

items.definition: Happening by chance rather than design. Often used loosely to mean 'lucky'.
items.etymology: From Latin fortuitus 'happening by chance', from fors 'chance, luck'.
items.example_sentence: Penicillin's discovery began with a fortuitous contamination of a culture plate.

items.definition: Fond of company and sociable; in biology, living in flocks or groups.
items.etymology: From Latin gregarius 'belonging to a flock', from grex 'flock, herd'.
items.example_sentence: Gregarious by nature, he knew everyone on the floor within a week.

items.definition: A person who attacks cherished beliefs or established institutions.
items.etymology: From Medieval Greek eikonoklastes 'image-breaker', from eikon 'image' and klan 'to break'; first applied to opponents of religious images in the Byzantine Empire.
items.example_sentence: An iconoclast in her field, she questioned a model everyone else took for granted.

items.definition: A habit, behavior or way of thinking peculiar to one person or thing.
items.etymology: From Greek idiosynkrasia 'peculiar temperament', from idios 'one's own' and synkrasis 'mixture'.
items.example_sentence: One idiosyncrasy of the old code base is that every date is stored as text.

items.definition: Acting quickly and without thought or care for consequences.
items.etymology: From Late Latin impetuosus, from impetus 'attack, force'.
items.example_sentence: An impetuous purchase at midnight became a regret by morning.

items.definition: Not harmful or offensive; often so mild as to go unnoticed.
items.etymology: From Latin innocuus, from in- 'not' and nocuus 'harmful', from nocere 'to harm'.
items.example_sentence: The bug began as an innocuous warning that everyone ignored.

items.definition: Sluggish and lacking energy or enthusiasm.
items.etymology: From Greek lethargikos, from lethargos 'forgetful', from lethe 'forgetfulness'.
items.example_sentence: A heavy lunch left the whole seminar lethargic by two o'clock.

items.definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
items.etymology: From Latin magnanimus 'great-souled', from magnus 'great' and animus 'soul, mind'.
items.example_sentence: The winner was magnanimous, crediting her opponent's strategy in the interview.

items.definition: Showing great care and precision about every detail.
items.etymology: From Latin meticulosus 'fearful, timid', from metus 'fear'; the sense 'careful about details' developed in the 19th century.
items.example_sentence: Meticulous lab notes made the experiment easy to reproduce.

items.definition: Appearing casually calm and relaxed; showing no concern or anxiety.
items.etymology: From French nonchalant, from non- 'not' and chaloir 'to be concerned', from Latin calere 'to be warm'.
items.example_sentence: He gave a nonchalant shrug when the server crashed mid-demo.

items.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change an opinion or course of action.
items.etymology: From Latin obduratus, past participle of obdurare 'to harden', from ob 'against' and durus 'hard'.
items.example_sentence: The committee remained obdurate despite new evidence.

items.definition: The presence of something in only small or insufficient amounts.
items.etymology: From Latin paucitas 'fewness', from paucus 'few'.
items.example_sentence: The paucity of long-term data limits what the study can conclude.
